title: Acceptance counts: A social psychological perspective on young men’s responses to baldness
abstract: Objectives Male pattern balding is a common and benign process. However, some men report intense distress because of it. Consistent with transactional coping theory and the idea of coping norms, this distress may not necessarily arise from baldness itself but rather from social judgments of men’s responses to baldness. Across four studies (total N = 686 young adults aged 18 to 35 years; 61% women), the present research investigated which ways of responding to baldness were perceived as appropriate (Studies 1a and 1b) and to what extent appropriate responses to baldness affected social attractiveness judgments (Studies 2a and 2b). Methods and Results Studies 1a and 1b revealed that participants mostly recommended a hypothetical male friend to accept his baldness or to pursue medical services (e.g., using pharmaceuticals), with the latter recommendation still relatively frequently given even when participants knew about the benign character of baldness. Recommendations for cosmetic services (e.g., using special shampoos) and compensation (e.g., gaining muscle) were less frequently made, and avoidance (e.g., of mirrors) was never recommended. Assessing impression formation, participants of Studies 2a and 2b rated balding men who accepted their baldness as most, and avoidant men as least, socially attractive. Compensating men and men pursuing medical or cosmetic services were ranked as moderately socially attractive. Participant gender was controlled for in all analyses. Conclusions Collectively, these results suggest acceptance of baldness is judged most appropriate and makes the most favorable social impression, offering an important counter to commercialized baldness treatment.
